title: Creating Your First Node.js Project
learning_outcomes: Describe Project initialization and explain how it relates to Creating Your First Node.js Project.
Demonstrate Basic folder structure in a small Node.js example and predict the observable result.
Test a failure, boundary, lifecycle, or version-compatibility case involving Creating a package manifest.

content.intro: Creating Your First Node.js Project is part of getting started and working with the runtime. This lesson connects Project initialization, Basic folder structure, Creating a package manifest to a concrete Node.js example. Focus on the behavior you can observe, the assumptions the API makes, and one failure or boundary case.
content.why_it_matters: Node.js combines the JavaScript language engine with APIs for interacting with the host environment. Run a tiny script with the selected Node.js executable and compare the output to the documented expectation.

const project = { name: 'first-node-app', type: 'module', scripts: { start: 'node src/main.mjs' } };
console.log(project.type, project.scripts.start);
content_blocks.run_instructions: Inspect this JavaScript in a local Node.js project. It is a static-validation teaching example: CodeLeaf does not run this arbitrary example in the API process. If it needs a package, file, server, database, or external service, provision that dependency in a separate local project and follow its official setup instructions. Run with `node example.mjs` when the example is self-contained, or adapt the required imports/inputs first.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the starting snippet and inputs. Repeat with one different valid value and one invalid, missing, empty, or failure input appropriate to the example.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with the code shown above. Predict the result before running it, then verify it against: An object is logged with runtime set to 'node' and version set to the installed Node.js version. Change one input or simulate one failure and describe how the behavior should change. Run a tiny script with the selected Node.js executable and compare the output to the documented expectation.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety note
content_blocks.text: Teaching baseline: use a supported Node.js LTS release (Node.js 24 LTS as checked on 2026-10-13). The official releases page lists Node.js 26 as Current and Node.js 24/22 as LTS. Some advanced APIs, flags, permission behavior, embedded SQLite capabilities, module-loader hooks, and TypeScript integration are version-sensitive; verify the exact installed runtime. The Node.js 22 runtime available in the build-check environment is used only for syntax checks. This example is for learning and static validation, not for executing untrusted learner code inside CodeLeaf.

content.task: Create or inspect a small Node.js example for Creating Your First Node.js Project. Include at least one listed subtopic, document the expected result, and verify a normal case plus a boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates a named lesson concept, rather than only mentioning the title.
Expected output or observable behavior is documented and reproducible.
At least one invalid, empty, timeout, resource, or failure case is handled or explained.
The solution does not put secrets in source code and does not execute untrusted code inside the production API process.
hints: Start with Project initialization; identify the input, operation, and observable result.
Run the smallest relevant example in the selected Node.js release before adding frameworks or external services.
Test one failure or boundary case for Basic folder structure, then explain why the outcome is expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating Node.js as a separate programming language or assuming browser-only APIs exist in Node.js.
common_mistakes.why: The code may pass a simple demonstration yet fail with real inputs, resource limits, timing, or runtime differences.
common_mistakes.fix: Identify whether each API belongs to JavaScript itself, Node.js, the browser, or a third-party dependency.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without checking its runtime, dependencies, input assumptions, or cleanup behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Node.js APIs and surrounding ecosystem tools have explicit version, trust, and resource boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: State the environment and dependency assumptions, then rerun the example from a clean starting state.
